1. Core Clinical Tension: A 66-year-old diabetic male presents with subacute constitutional decline (fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, abdominal distension), followed by high-grade spikes of fever up to 39 °C and night sweats. Abdominal CT reveals a massive 13 cm well-defined cystic renal mass causing hydronephrosis and parenchymal atrophy, radiologically reported as consistent with a cystic nephroma. The clinical tension lies in resolving whether this mass represents a primary cystic renal malignancy with paraneoplastic systemic features versus an infectious renal pseudotumor or giant abscess caused by mycobacterial infection co-infected with enteric bacilli.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint falls at the conclusion of initial emergency evaluation and imaging (physical examination, initial hematologic/inflammatory markers, urinalysis, negative routine blood/urine cultures, and abdominal CT imaging), immediately prior to ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration, pigtail drainage, and microbiological testing of the cystic fluid.
3. Differential Distinctions: Cystic nephroma or cystic renal cell carcinoma presents in older adults with large multicystic renal masses, hematuria, or flank fullness, but typically does not cause acute fever reaching 39 °C, drenching night sweats, and marked elevations in systemic inflammatory markers. Isolated pyogenic renal abscess (e.g., uncomplicated Escherichia coli pyonephrosis) presents with high fever, acute flank pain, and pyuria, but standard urine cultures are often positive and it rarely manifests as an indolent 13 cm chronic cystic mass without pre-existing urinary tract symptoms unless driven by an underlying granulomatous mycobacterial infection.
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with a medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and a known left renal cortical cyst presented to the emergency department with a 15-day history of profound fatigue, anorexia, involuntary weight loss, and abdominal distension. Over the four days prior to presentation, he developed intermittent high fevers reaching 39 °C accompanied by drenching night sweats. He denied chest pain, cough, dyspnea, dysuria, hematuria, or focal neurological symptoms, and reported no history of substance use, recent foreign travel, or known exposure to chronic infectious diseases.

On physical examination, he was drowsy and sluggish but oriented to person, place, and time, and arousable to light voice. He was tachycardic with a heart rate of 105 beats per minute; other vital signs were normal. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. Pulmonary auscultation revealed fine end-inspiratory crackles over the left lung base. The abdomen was soft and visibly distended without shifting dullness, peritoneal signs, or focal organomegaly, and no peripheral edema was observed.

Initial laboratory workup demonstrated markedly elevated systemic inflammatory markers (elevated C-reactive protein and ESR). Urinalysis was completely normal without pyuria, bacteriuria, or microhematuria. Rapid HIV serology was non-reactive. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen demonstrated a large, well-defined, 13 cm cystic lesion replacing the left kidney, reported as radiologically consistent with a cystic nephroma, associated with mild ipsilateral hydronephrosis and severe renal parenchymal thinning. Routine aerobic and anaerobic blood and urine cultures showed no bacterial growth.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Cystic Renal Neoplasm (e.g., Multilocular Cystic Nephroma or Cystic Renal Cell Carcinoma)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Initially suggested by abdominal CT imaging showing a 13 cm well-demarcated cystic lesion with parenchymal compression in an elderly diabetic male with B-symptoms, but ruled out when aspirated fluid analysis showed infectious purulent fluid with positive microbiological cultures rather than malignant cells.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: An abdominal computed tomography (CT) was performed, showing a well-defined left cystic renal mass (13 cm) consistent with a cystic nephroma, associated with mild hydronephrosis and renal parenchymal atrophy

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute Pyogenic Renal Abscess / Isolated Escherichia coli Pyonephrosis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to high fever, tachycardia, elevated inflammatory markers, and the eventual isolation of E. coli from the cystic fluid, but ruled out as the primary etiology because the patient had an indolent 15-day course, sterile initial urinalysis and urine cultures, and simultaneous recovery of acid-fast mycobacteria that had established the underlying cavitary renal lesion.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Escherichia coli and M. tuberculosis were both isolated from the sample (Table 2).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The definitive turning point occurred when the patient underwent ultrasound-guided percutaneous puncture and drainage of the renal cystic lesion, with microbiological analysis of the aspirate successfully isolating Mycobacterium tuberculosis alongside co-infecting Escherichia coli, confirming renal tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: During hospitalization, the patient underwent ultrasound-guided drainage and aspiration of the renal mass, after which a 12F pigtail catheter was placed for continuous drainage. The aspirated fluid was sent for cytological and microbiological analysis, including testing for M. tuberculosis. Escherichia coli and M. tuberculosis were both isolated from the sample

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case following Stanford MedCaseReasoning. Breakpoint stops following abdominal CT and routine blood/urine cultures prior to percutaneous aspiration. Zero spoilers in case_prompt. Candidates and Diagnostic Pivot supported by verbatim quotes.
